title: Integration of symmetric two-cocycles on disjoint subsets
statement:
Let $E$ be a finite set [def-sfb-finite-infinite-set] and $A$ a commutative group, written multiplicatively with identity $1$ (multiplication is associative and commutative, $1a=a$, and every $a$ has an inverse $a^{-1}$ with $a^{-1}a=1$). For each ordered pair of disjoint subsets $U,V\subseteq E$ let $q(U,V)\in A$ be given. Assume $q(U,V)=q(V,U)$, $q(\varnothing,V)=1$, and, for all three pairwise disjoint subsets $U,V,W\subseteq E$,
$$q(U,V)q(U\cup V,W)=q(V,W)q(U,V\cup W).$$
Then there exists a function $b:\mathcal P(E)\to A$, where $\mathcal P(E)$ denotes the set of subsets of $E$, such that $b(B)=1$ whenever $|B|\leq1$ and, for all disjoint $U,V\subseteq E$,
$$q(U,V)=\frac{b(U\cup V)}{b(U)b(V)}.$$
Division means multiplication by inverses. No divisibility or torsion condition on $A$ is assumed.

proof.text: Induct on the number of elements of the finite set $E$ [def-sfb-finite-infinite-set], with the induction assertion quantified over all cocycles satisfying the stated hypotheses. If $E=\varnothing$, put $b(\varnothing)=1$; the only pair is $(\varnothing,\varnothing)$ and its required equation is $1=1$. For nonempty $E$ choose $x\in E$ and put $F=E\setminus\{x\}$. Restriction of $q$ to disjoint subsets of $F$ retains symmetry, normalization and the three-block identity. Since $|F|<|E|$, induction gives $b_0:\mathcal P(F)\to A$ with $b_0(B)=1$ for $|B|\leq1$ and $b_0(R\cup S)=q(R,S)b_0(R)b_0(S)$ for disjoint $R,S\subseteq F$.

source.place: Paragraph (3), auxiliary algebra below the cubical-line coherence input: integrate the two-variable cocycle obtained by fixing a singleton in the third argument. Agent-written finite-set lemma; not claimed as a theorem in this blueprint.

proof.text: For every $B\subseteq E$ define $b(B)=b_0(B)$ if $x\notin B$, and $b(B)=b_0(B\setminus\{x\})q(B\setminus\{x\},\{x\})$ if $x\in B$. Both arguments of $q$ in the second formula are disjoint subsets of $E$, so this defines a function on the entire power set. Its empty-set value and its singleton values away from $x$ are $1$ by the properties of $b_0$. At $\{x\}$ its value is $b_0(\varnothing)q(\varnothing,\{x\})=1$. Thus every required normalization holds.

proof.text: If instead $x\in U$, disjointness gives $x\notin V$, so apply the preceding case to $(V,U)$. Symmetry gives $q(V,U)=q(U,V)$; commutativity in $A$ and $V\cup U=U\cup V$ identify its quotient with the required one. These cases exhaust disjoint pairs, since $x$ cannot lie in both. The constructed $b$ therefore completes the induction. Only multiplication and inversion in $A$ have been used, so no roots, divisibility, or torsion hypothesis is needed.
